name: Rhaponticum carthamoides (maral root)

lead: Maral root is a Siberian alpine herb whose roots contain large amounts of 20-hydroxyecdysone, an insect molting hormone. Supplement sellers promote it for strength, recovery and stress resistance.
The published literature is mainly chemistry and lab work; the sources reviewed contain no human trial of it for muscle or appearance.

paras: The claimed mechanism rests on its ecdysteroid content. Reviews describe antioxidant and other activities in laboratory settings; effects in people have not been established in the sources reviewed.
Safety data in humans are not covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a supplement, and products can be confused with Rheum rhaponticum, a different plant.

lead: Rhaponticum carthamoides (synonym Leuzea carthamoides), known as maral root, is a perennial herb of the daisy family (Asteraceae) that grows wild in southern Siberia, Kazakhstan, the Altai and the western Sayan Mountains at sub-alpine and alpine elevations.[1] Its roots are rich in 20-hydroxyecdysone, an ecdysteroid that acts as a molting hormone in arthropods.[1][2]

It is sold as an adaptogen and, in muscle-building circles, as a source of ecdysteroids. Published literature on the plant is mostly phytochemical and pharmacological reviews, with in vitro and animal work; the sources available for this article identify no completed human trial of maral root for muscle or appearance outcomes.[2][3]
infobox: Southern Siberia, Kazakhstan, Altai, western Sayan[1]

paras: The common name maral root is said to come from the maral deer, which reportedly eat the plant, though this etymology is not firmly sourced.[1] The species is described as grown in cultivation in Russia and Eastern Europe.[1]

A 2009 review in Phytochemistry catalogued the plant's chemistry and pharmacology, including ecdysteroids, flavonoids and other constituents, and summarised reported biological activities.[2] Other studies have reported antimicrobial activity of crude extracts from Siberian medicinal plants including this species, and identified radical-scavenging compounds in it.[4][5]
Reviews of adaptogens list Rhaponticum carthamoides among plants studied for stress-protective properties, mostly in cell and animal models.[3][6]

No studies found for maral root in muscle growth, recovery or appearance. Related research is limited to laboratory and animal work on the plant and its constituents, and to trials of a different plant, Rheum rhaponticum (rhubarb extract ERr 731), which has a confusingly similar name and was tested in menopausal women.[7]

sections.h: Use in muscle and recovery communities
paras: Supplement sellers market maral root as an ecdysteroid and adaptogen for strength and recovery. The ecdysteroid class is the basis of these claims; the sources reviewed here contain no human trial results supporting or refuting them.

lore.intro: Maral root is mentioned in supplement and muscle-building contexts as a plant ecdysteroid source and adaptogen.
